extracted.intended_audience: authors, peer reviewers, and journal editors preparing or assessing health/rehabilitation research manuscripts (systematic reviews, RCTs, observational studies, n-of-1/single-case designs, diagnostic studies, and qualitative studies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying reporting guidelines and method-quality rating scales when preparing or peer-reviewing health research manuscripts (systematic reviews, randomized trials, observational studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, single-case designs, and qualitative research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines provide a brief, concise and practical ‘user’s guide’ to publishing reports. The guides include a descriptive checklist which contains a minimum core set of essential items that an author is expected to address when publishing an article — i.e., what needs to be reported and how it should be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines improve clarity and transparency of report writing; they assist readers, reviewers and editors to critically appraise an article; they typically publish both a short checklist and an extended 'explanation and elaboration' paper with rationale and model examples. They are not intended to be a 'how to do it' manual (they do not prescribe specific statistical techniques) and are not intended to be evaluative recommendations about study design and conduct. Checklist items should be addressed in sufficient detail and with clarity somewhere in an article, but the order and format may vary with journal style and field traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRISMA statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 27-item checklist delineating criteria authors should address 'to ensure clear presentation of what was planned, done, and found in a systematic review' covering title, abstract, introduction, methods (12 items), results (7 items), discussion (3 items), and funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key items include identifying report as a systematic review/meta-analysis; providing structured summary; stating rationale and explicit questions (PICOS); protocol registration; eligibility criteria; information sources and full electronic search strategy; study selection process; data collection process; data items and assumptions; methods for assessing risk of bias in individual studies and across studies; principal summary measures; synthesis methods (including measures of consistency); presentation of study screening numbers with reasons (flow diagram); presentation of study characteristics, risk of bias within studies, results of individual studies and meta-analyses (including effect estimates and CIs), additional analyses, summary of evidence and limitations, conclusions and funding. PRISMA references: Moher et al. (2009); elaboration: Liberati et al. (2009). PRISMA is designed for systematic reviews (often of RCTs) though related guidelines (e.g., MOOSE) address observational study meta-analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: AMSTAR (Assessment of Multiple Systematic Reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 11-item method quality scale designed for assessing systematic reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed with content validity via statistical item reduction and expert review. Reports excellent inter-rater reliability for total score (kw = .84), moderate to perfect for individual items (Kw = .51–1.00). Completion time reported as about 15 minutes per report. Use AMSTAR to evaluate methodological quality of systematic reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: CONSORT statement (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2010
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline for randomized controlled trials: a 25-item checklist (37 total components) covering title/abstract, introduction, methods (17 items), results (10 items), discussion (3 items), and other information (3 items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items include: identification as a randomized trial in the title; structured abstract; background and objectives; trial design (e.g., parallel, factorial) including allocation ratio and important changes after commencement; eligibility criteria and settings; detailed interventions allowing replication; completely defined prespecified primary and secondary outcomes and assessment timing; sample size determination and interim analyses/stopping guidelines; methods of random sequence generation, type of randomization (blocking/stratification), allocation concealment mechanism and implementation (who generated sequence, who enrolled participants, who assigned interventions); blinding (who was blinded and how); statistical methods for primary/secondary outcomes and additional analyses; participant flow (diagram strongly recommended) with numbers assigned, receiving treatment, analysed and reasons for losses/exclusions; recruitment dates; baseline data; numbers analysed and whether by original assigned groups; outcome results with effect sizes and precision (CIs), recommended presentation of absolute and relative effects for binary outcomes; ancillary analyses and harms; trial limitations, generalisability, balanced interpretation, registration number, protocol access and funding sources. CONSORT emphasizes a participant flow diagram to report conduct and attrition. Refer to Schulz et al. (2010) and CONSORT explanation/elaboration (Moher et al., 2010).

rubrics_metrics.name: CONSORT Extension for Nonpharmacologic Treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Additions/modifications to the standard CONSORT checklist to address nonpharmacologic trials (e.g., behavioural, surgical), covering allocation, title/abstract content, eligibility of centres and care providers, intervention details, standardisation, adherence, clustering by providers/centres, and reporting of care-provider characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension items include precise details of both experimental treatment and comparator, description of intervention components and tailoring, details of how interventions were standardised and how adherence of care providers was assessed or enhanced; reporting whether participants, those administering interventions, and outcome assessors were blinded (or not) and methods used; how clustering by care providers/centres was addressed; number of care providers/centres in each group and patients per provider/centre; details of implementation of intervention and allocation of care providers. A corresponding 10-item method quality scale (CLEAR NPT) was developed (Boutron et al., 2005) with ~10 minutes completion time.

rubrics_metrics.name: PEDro scale (Physiotherapy Evidence Database)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 11-item scale that uses 10 items to produce a method quality score for randomized controlled trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely used for RCTs in physiotherapy/rehabilitation. Reported acceptable inter-rater reliability for total score (ICC = .68) and individual items (k = .50 to .79). Useful as a quick method-quality checklist when assessing RCT reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: CENT (CONSORT Extension for N-of-1 Trials) (emerging)
rubrics_metrics.description: A planned CONSORT extension specific to n-of-1 trials (single-participant designs) being developed to provide reporting guidance for n-of-1 trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CENT will join recommended statements for journals when published. N-of-1 trials (single-case experimental designs, SCED) are rigorous, a priori methodological designs involving systematic observation, manipulation, repeated measurement and data analysis; now regarded as Level 1 evidence for individual patient decisions by Oxford CEBM.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCED Scale (Single-case Experimental Design Scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 11-item scale (10 items used for a total method-quality score) to rate methodological quality of single-case experimental designs and n-of-1 trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SCED Scale has good inter-rater reliability for total score (ICC = .88) and fair-to-perfect for individual items (k = .48 to 1.0). Administration time generally 15–20 minutes. Version 2 includes minor revisions and an added item.

rubrics_metrics.name: STROBE statement (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 22-item checklist addressing reporting of observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) covering title/abstract, introduction, methods (9 items), results (5 items), discussion (4 items), and other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key items include: indicate study design in title/abstract; provide balanced abstract; explain background and objectives; present key elements of study design early; describe setting, locations, relevant dates (recruitment, follow-up); eligibility criteria and selection methods for cohort/case-control/cross-sectional designs (including matching criteria when applicable); clearly define outcomes, exposures, predictors, confounders and effect modifiers; describe sources of data and measurement methods; efforts to address bias; explanation of study size; handling of quantitative variables; full description of statistical methods (including confounding control, subgroups, missing data, loss to follow-up, sampling strategy, sensitivity analyses); report participant numbers at each stage with reasons (flow diagram recommended); descriptive data, missing data counts, follow-up time; outcome data appropriate to design; unadjusted and adjusted estimates with precision (95% CI) and which confounders were adjusted for; category boundaries when continuous variables were categorised; consider translating relative risks to absolute risk when relevant. STROBE provides combined and design-specific checklists available from the STROBE website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downs & Black checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A method quality rating scale containing 26 items in four subscales: Reporting (10), Confounding (6), Bias (7) and External validity (3), suitable for observational studies (cohort and case-control) and randomized trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses both internal validity (bias, confounding) and external validity (generalisation). Reported inter-rater reliability moderate for total score (r = .75), subscale reliability varies (Bias r = .83; External validity r = -.14). Administration time averages 20–25 minutes (range 10–45). Use when assessing methodological quality across study designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: STARD statement (Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A checklist developed to improve reporting of studies of diagnostic accuracy, aimed at ensuring complete and accurate reporting of diagnostic accuracy studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed following concerns about poor methodological and reporting quality of diagnostic test studies. The STARD initiative produced a checklist and an explanation/elaboration paper; key aims include reporting study design, participants, test methods, reference standards, blinding/masking, and measures of diagnostic accuracy to allow assessment and replication. See Bossuyt et al. (2003a, 2003b).

rubrics_metrics.name: QUADAS (and QUADAS-2) — quality assessment of diagnostic accuracy studies
rubrics_metrics.description: A tool for the quality assessment of diagnostic accuracy studies included in systematic reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QUADAS was developed to evaluate methodological quality of diagnostic accuracy studies for inclusion in systematic reviews. Evaluations of QUADAS have been published (development and reproducibility); apply these tools to assess bias and applicability concerns in diagnostic accuracy studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: JBI-QARI critical appraisal instrument (for qualitative research)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 10-item critical appraisal instrument for qualitative research focusing on philosophical and methodological congruity, explication of researcher biases, and representation of participants' perspectives and their relationship to conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JBI-QARI items cover 3 areas: philosophical/methodological congruity (5 items), researcher bias explication (2 items), and representation of participants’ perspectives and links to conclusions (3 items). Use as one instrument among others to appraise qualitative studies for inclusion in evidence synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: COREQ (Consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 32-item checklist for interviews and focus groups intended to standardise reporting of qualitative studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COREQ covers domains such as research team and reflexivity, study design, and data analysis and reporting. Use to improve transparency and completeness of qualitative research reports (Tong, Sainsbury & Craig, 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to report ethics approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not included in all checklists, ethical approval to conduct research on human participants is generally necessary and the journal requires authors to include a statement about ethics approval to conduct their study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should include an ethics approval statement (and animal ethics where applicable) in manuscripts. Even when checklists omit ethics explicitly, journals commonly require this information for peer review and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting guidelines by reviewers and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Brain Impairment endorses the described reporting guidelines and applies them within the review process; reviewers and editors will use these standards when assessing submissions and authors are strongly encouraged to adhere to relevant guideline items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist items need to be addressed somewhere in the article with sufficient detail and clarity; adherence assists critical appraisal of internal/external validity, clinical relevance, and contribution to literature. Guidelines are evolving documents and should be updated as new information emerges. The EQUATOR Network is recommended as a resource and library of reporting guidelines.
